extracted.intended_audience: readers of historical/biographical essays on American naturalists and abolitionist households (general educated public, historians)
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from a 19th-century biographical/historical essay describing the life, methods, and character of naturalist Thaddeus W. Harris and a later piece on John Brown's household; not an instruction manual but it contains evaluative statements about scientific practice and specimen care. Useful as a primary-source style example of scientific conduct and popular-science writing of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making entomology popular (plain-language introduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewritten my introduction in plain and simple language, divested as much as possible of all hard words, and intend to add to it brief descriptions of some of our most common insects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target young readers to excite a taste for the subject so parents become interested; keep language simple, avoid hard vocabulary, and include brief, accessible descriptions of common species. The aim is usefulness and entertainment for the intended (juvenile) audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Card-catalogue method for insect collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Catalogues were made on the plan of the card catalogues now used in libraries, upon uniform pieces of paper, three or four inches square, which he afterwards tied in bundles and carefully labeled. Each card contained the name of the insect, with synonyms and authorities, and the number it bore in his catalogue, — but no description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uniform cards with standardized fields (name, synonyms, authorities, catalogue number); tie and label bundles; keep manuscripts/indices neat and clear for institutional custody (examples: Say's collection catalogued in same manner; manuscripts retained by the Boston Society).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimen preservation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The delicate and systematic care with which Dr. Harris preserved his insects has secured for them a permanent usefulness. Almost all his American insects remain labeled and arranged as he left them, thus fixing firmly and indisputably every step he made in their classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve specimens with careful labeling and arrangement to ensure long-term usefulness; avoid loose pins, detached labels, larvae infestation, and crushing during transport—poor preservation renders specimens 'absolutely worthless.' Pack and maintain collections so they remain a standard of comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fieldwork as essential to natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: No man knew better than Dr. Harris that the best work of a naturalist must be done out of doors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize in-situ observation and collecting: be prepared to convert everyday items into collecting tools (e.g., umbrella into a net, hat into a collecting-box), work by lantern at night, search beneath bark in late seasons, and undertake effective excursions even if infrequent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of detailed illustration for classification and life-history
rubrics_metrics.description: He learned to classify butterflies by drawing the nervures of their wings, so he fixed by copying each successive stage of development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ accurate drawings of morphological details and successive developmental stages to aid classification and trace transformations from egg to adult; pencil skill and illustrative record are essential tools for natural-history documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific character: qualities constituting a strong scientific reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: He combined a fidelity that never shrank from the most laborious details with an intellectual activity that always looked beyond details to principles. He had also the modesty and unselfishness of science, and he had what may be called its chivalry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate diligence in detailed work along with the ability to generalize to principles; maintain modesty, unselfishness, and collegiality (e.g., assisting younger entomologists by arranging and labeling their collections; defending peers' priority and work). Moral qualities are part of scientific excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and permanence of observational records
rubrics_metrics.description: No series of observations made by him ever needed revision or verification by another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for observational accuracy and methodological rigor such that records are reliable and enduring; meticulous recording and preservation of both specimens and notes reduce the need for later verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neat, clear transcription and archival care of correspondence/manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: This institution also holds copies of almost all his entomological letters, transcribed with a neatness and clearness peculiarly his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcribe and maintain correspondence/manuscripts with clarity and neatness to facilitate future use by institutions and researchers; deposit such materials with learned societies or libraries for preservation.
